question: How can a recurrent network learn to bridge very long time lags when backpropagated error vanishes or blows up exponentially?
hypothesis: Enforcing constant error flow through self-connected linear units (constant error carousels) guarded by multiplicative gates, with gradient truncated at cell boundaries, lets gradient descent bridge lags above 1000 steps.
contributions: Analysis (after Hochreiter 1991) that error backflow in BPTT/RTRL decays or explodes exponentially with lag
LSTM: memory cell with constant error carousel (CEC), multiplicative input and output gates, memory cell blocks
Efficient truncated RTRL-style gradient with O(W) update complexity per time step, local in space and time
Experiments on artificial long-time-lag tasks with comparisons to RTRL, BPTT, RCC, Elman nets, neural sequence chunker

method.summary: LSTM is a three-layer network (input, one fully connected hidden layer of memory cell blocks with input and output gates, output) trained by online gradient descent using a truncated RTRL variant in which error is not propagated out of cells or gates. Six families of artificial tasks (embedded Reber grammar, noise-free/noisy long-lag sequences, two-sequence classification, adding, multiplication, temporal order) are used, mostly with minimal lags of 50 to 1000 steps.
method.task: learning long-time-lag dependencies in sequences (synthetic benchmarks)

datasets.name: Embedded Reber grammar (Exp 1)
datasets.split: three random train/test pairs, 10 trials each (30 trials)
datasets.source: generated by grammar (Smith & Zipser 1989; Cleeremans et al. 1989; Fahlman 1991)
datasets.preprocessing: local one-hot, 7 input and 7 output units; test strings exclude training strings

datasets.name: Tasks 2a/2b/2c noise-free and noisy long-lag sequences
datasets.size: 2a: two sequences; 2b: two classes of random sequences; 2c: random sequences, expected length q+14; 10,000 successive test sequences
datasets.preprocessing: locally represented symbols; 2a/2b p+1 inputs, 2c p+4 inputs and 2 outputs

datasets.name: Task 3 two-sequence problems (3a, 3b, 3c)
datasets.preprocessing: single real-valued input line; gaussian noise variance 0.2 after the first N elements; 3b also noise on first N; 3c targets 0.2/0.8 with noise variance 0.1

datasets.name: Adding problem (Exp 4)
datasets.preprocessing: pairs (value in [-1,1], marker); target 0.5+(X1+X2)/4.0; length between T and T+T/10

datasets.name: Temporal order (Exp 6a/6b)
datasets.preprocessing: length 100-110; 4 classes (6a) or 8 classes (6b); symbols {a,b,c,d} plus X/Y, E start, B trigger

models.name: LSTM
models.params: 93 to 10,504 weights depending on task (Table 10, e.g. 264/276 Exp 1, 93 Exp 4/5, 156 task 6a, 308 task 6b, 6064 task 2c q=1000)
models.architecture: 3-layer recurrent net: input, fully connected hidden layer of memory cell blocks with input and output gates, output layer connected to memory cells only
models.hidden: Exp 1: 3 blocks size 2 or 4 blocks size 1; 2a/2b: 1 cell; 2c: 2 blocks size 1; 3: 3 blocks size 1; 4/5: 2 blocks size 2; 6a: 2 blocks size 2; 6b: 3 blocks size 2

other.activations: gates and output unit logistic sigmoid [0,1]; h range [-1,1]: h(x)=2/(1+exp(-x))-1; g range [-2,2]: g(x)=4/(1+exp(-x))-2 (Appendix A.1)
other.bias: initial gate biases negative to avoid abuse and state drift, e.g. output gate bias -1,-2,-3 (Exp 1); see Table 10 col 10-11

models.name: RTRL
models.architecture: fully recurrent net (one self-recurrent hidden unit in task 2a)

other.source: Exp 1 results taken from Smith & Zipser 1989
results taken from Cleeremans et al. 1989

training.objective: squared error E(t)=sum_k (t_k(t)-y_k(t))^2 (A.14); error signals only at sequence end except Exp 1 and 2a/2b (every step)
training.optimizer: online gradient descent with truncated RTRL-style gradient (plain SGD, no momentum mentioned)
training.batch_size: 1 (online learning, one sequence at a time)
training.steps: stop at success criteria, e.g. 2a/2b/2c capped at 5 million sequence presentations; see Table 11
training.seq_len: minimal lag 9 (Exp 1) up to 1000 (task 2c); T=100 to 1000 in Exp 3/4
training.regularisation: none stated; negative gate biases against abuse and state drift
training.seeds: different random weight initialisations; trial counts per experiment: Exp 1 30 (three train/test pairs x 10), tasks 2a and 2b 18, task 2c 20, Exp 3 10, Exp 4 10, Exp 5 10, task 6a 20, task 6b 10

other.activation_reset: net activations reset after each processed sequence
other.stopping_criteria: Exp 4/6: ST3(beta): average training error below beta (0.01 / 0.1) and 2000 most recent sequences processed correctly; Exp 3 ST1/ST2; Exp 5 nseq=140 and 13 (see text)
other.abuse_problem: solutions: sequential network construction (2a/2b) or negative output gate bias

metrics.name: success after (sequence presentations)
metrics.definition: number of training sequences presented until the stopping criterion is met, mean over trials

metrics.name: % successful trials
metrics.definition: fraction of trials meeting the task's success criterion (e.g. max abs error below 0.25 over 10,000 test sequences in 2a; all training and test symbols predicted correctly in Exp 1)

metrics.name: wrong predictions
metrics.definition: test sequences (of 2560) with error above 0.04 (Exp 4/5), 0.3 (Exp 6), or 0.2 (Exp 3)

eval.protocol: Mean over trials with different weight initialisations; no significance tests; baseline results in Exp 1 taken from the cited papers; BPTT only in task 2a, RTRL elsewhere then omitted for longer lags

availability.data: synthetic tasks generated from textual descriptions

evidence.quote: We always use online learning (as opposed to batch learning) and logistic sigmoids as activation functions.

evidence.where: Sect 4.1 (no forget gate in the original LSTM)

limits: Truncated LSTM will not easily solve strongly delayed XOR problems (nondecomposable tasks) (Sect 6.1).
Behaves like a feedforward net seeing the whole input; 500-step parity solvable by weight guessing but not by truncated LSTM (Sect 6.1).
Cannot count discrete time steps precisely; extra counting mechanism needed (Sect 6.1).
Each block needs two extra gate units; weights up to 9x (text also says factor of 32 in fully connected case).
Experiments are artificial; real-world application (time series, music, speech) left as future work (Sect 7).
Several benchmarks (3a, 3b, Bengio et al. tasks) are solved faster by random weight guessing, as the authors concede.
Architectures were 'selected quite arbitrarily'; no ablations beyond output gate in Exp 1; no hardware, compute or wall-clock reported; no code released.
Original formulation has no forget gate and no output-side training tricks later standard; the truncated gradient is not full BPTT through gates.
